pos: n. (a skilled workman; a craftsman in metal, stone, or timber)
etymology: Latin artifex, from ars, art, and facere, to make. The Authorized Version uses it for the master craftsman as distinct from the common labourer.
biblical_def: The first artificer named in Scripture stands in the line of Cain: “Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron” (Gen 4:22). Metalworking, music, and the building of cities all appear in Cain's line before the flood, and the Bible reports this without embarrassment. Common grace is real: the arts were given to men, and men under judgment still received them. Isaiah then lists “the cunning artificer” among the pillars of Judah's civil order which the LORD would take away in the day of judgment — the mighty man, the man of war, the judge, the prophet, the prudent, the ancient, the captain of fifty, the honourable man, the counsellor, the cunning artificer, and the eloquent orator (Isa 3:2-3). To remove the skilled craftsmen from a nation is a judgment, because a society that cannot make anything cannot long defend or feed itself. And the highest use of the word's idea is at the tabernacle, where the LORD names Bezaleel and says, I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship. The first man in Scripture said to be filled with the Spirit of God is a craftsman.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines an artificer as an artist; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge of a particular kind; also a contriver, an inventor.
webster_full: ARTIFICER, n. An artist; a mechanic or manufacturer; one whose occupation requires skill or knowledge of a particular kind; as a silversmith or a carpenter.
2. One who makes or contrives; an inventor.
3. In the army, a soldier employed in the mechanical trades.
scriptures: Gen 4:22
And Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubalcain was Naamah.
Isa 3:3
The captain of fifty, and the honourable man, and the counsellor, and the cunning artificer, and the eloquent orator.
Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,
corruption_summary: Manual and technical skill has been quietly demoted beneath academic and professional work, a ranking Scripture nowhere makes and Exodus 31 flatly contradicts.
corruption_paragraphs: Exodus 31:1-5 is the passage that ought to have settled this permanently. The first man in the Bible of whom it is said that God filled him with His Spirit is not a prophet, a priest, or a king: it is Bezaleel the son of Uri, and the filling is specified as wisdom, understanding, knowledge, and all manner of workmanship — in cutting of stones, to set them, and in carving of timber. Aholiab is given with him, and the Spirit's gift includes the ability to teach the trade to others (Exo 35:34). Our culture has arranged work in a hierarchy that Scripture does not recognise, in which the man who designs is above the man who builds and the man who advises is above them both, and it has arranged education to match, so that a generation was told that the trades were what happened to those who could not do better. The Reformers took the opposite view and taught it as doctrine: the milkmaid and the magistrate hold callings equally from God, and the question is faithfulness, not station. Paul made tents. The Lord Jesus was known in Nazareth as the carpenter. The line of Cain shows that skill without godliness produces Lamech and his sword-song; Exodus 31 shows that skill filled with the Spirit builds the house of God.
roots_summary: Hebrew charash (H2796), a craftsman, engraver, artificer in wood, stone, or metal; chakam-leb, wise-hearted, the tabernacle workers; chokmah (H2451), wisdom, which in Exodus includes manual skill.
roots_lines: Hebrew charash (H2796) — a craftsman or artificer; the same noun covers the smith, the mason, and the carver; Genesis 4:22, Isaiah 3:3, 1 Chronicles 29:5.
Hebrew chakam-leb — wise-hearted; the standing description of the tabernacle workmen, where wisdom is a skill of the hands; Exodus 28:3, 35:10.
Hebrew chokmah (H2451) — wisdom; used in Exodus 31:3 of craftsmanship, and in Proverbs of the fear of the LORD, one word for both; Exodus 31:3, Proverbs 9:10.
usage: “An instructer of every artificer in brass and iron” — the trades begin in the line of Cain, under common grace.
“The cunning artificer, and the eloquent orator” — removing the craftsmen is named as judgment on a nation.
“Filled him with the spirit of God…in all manner of workmanship” — the first Spirit-filled man in Scripture is a craftsman.

pos: n. (the skill of a workman; the thing made, considered as the product of that skill)
etymology: English workman and -ship, the suffix of condition or quality. The Greek poiema in Ephesians 2:10 is the noun behind English poem: a thing made.
biblical_def: Twice the word is used of the Spirit's gift to Bezaleel: “I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exo 31:3), repeated when Moses announces it to the congregation (Exo 35:31), with the particulars given in Exodus 31:5 — in cutting of stones, to set them, and in carving of timber. The tabernacle was not thrown together; it was made by a Spirit-filled artist to a pattern shewed in the mount. The word also has a dark use. Ahaz saw an altar at Damascus and sent Urijah the priest “the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof” (2Ki 16:10), and the brasen altar of the LORD was moved aside to make room for a copy of a pagan design. Excellent workmanship in the service of a borrowed religion is still apostasy. And Paul takes the idea to its height: “we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works” (Eph 2:10) — the Greek is poiema, His piece of work, His making. The believer is not the craftsman of his own salvation; he is the object on the bench.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines workmanship as the skill of a workman; the art or skill with which a thing is made; also the work performed; that which is effected by manual labor or skill.
webster_full: WORKMANSHIP, n. Manufacture; something produced by manual labor.
2. The skill of a workman; the execution or manner of making any thing.
3. That which is effected, made or produced; as, we are his workmanship. Eph. ii.
scriptures: Exo 31:3
And I have filled him with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship,

And king Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglathpileser king of Assyria, and saw an altar that was at Damascus: and king Ahaz sent to Urijah the priest the fashion of the altar, and the pattern of it, according to all the workmanship thereof.
Eph 2:10
For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus unto good works, which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them.
corruption_summary: Ephesians 2:10 is regularly quoted as a compliment to the reader — you are God's masterpiece — when Paul wrote it to explain why salvation cannot be of works.
corruption_paragraphs: Ephesians 2:10 has become a slogan of self-esteem, printed on wall art and read as a statement about the reader's inherent value: you are God's masterpiece. Paul's sentence is doing something quite different, and the connective word at its head shows it. Verses 8 and 9 have just said that by grace are ye saved through faith; and that not of yourselves: it is the gift of God: not of works, lest any man should boast. Verse 10 gives the reason: for we are his workmanship. The argument is that a made thing cannot take credit for its own making. The chapter began with dead in trespasses and sins, and the whole passage is about a creation out of nothing — created in Christ Jesus. Then the good works appear, not as the ground of salvation but as its purpose and God's prior appointment: which God hath before ordained that we should walk in them. Read as intended, the verse humbles before it comforts, and comforts far more deeply than the slogan does. A masterpiece that made itself would be an anxious thing, always needing to prove the claim. A workmanship is safe in the hands of the Workman, and Philippians 1:6 gives the guarantee: he which hath begun a good work in you will perform it until the day of Jesus Christ.
roots_summary: Hebrew mela'kah (H4399), work, occupation, workmanship; Greek poiema (G4161), a thing made, that which is fashioned; Greek ktizo (G2936), to create, of the new creation in Christ.
roots_lines: Hebrew mela'kah (H4399) — work, business, workmanship; the word for the tabernacle labour and for the work God rested from on the seventh day; Exodus 31:3, Genesis 2:2.
Greek poiema (G4161) — a thing made, a work; used twice, of the creation that leaves men without excuse and of the believer; Romans 1:20, Ephesians 2:10.
Greek ktizo (G2936) — to create; the new man created in righteousness and true holiness; Ephesians 2:10, 4:24, 2 Corinthians 5:17.
usage: “In all manner of workmanship” — the Spirit's gift to the tabernacle craftsman.
“According to all the workmanship thereof” — Ahaz copying a Damascus altar with excellent skill.
“We are his workmanship” — the reason salvation cannot be of works.

pos: n. pl. (those who draw water; in Joshua, the servile class assigned to the Gibeonites)
etymology: From draw, Old English dragan, to pull. “Hewers of wood and drawers of water” became a proverbial phrase in English for the lowest servile labour.
biblical_def: The Gibeonites came to Joshua with mouldy bread and clouted shoes, pretending to be from a far country, and Israel “asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD” but made a league with them. When the deceit came out, the oath still bound: “Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation” (Jos 9:21). Joshua pronounced the curse and the appointment together: “there shall none of you be freed from being bondmen, and hewers of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God” (Jos 9:23), and he “made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD…in the place which he should choose” (Jos 9:27). Two things follow, and both are large. First, an oath sworn in the LORD's name binds even when it was obtained by fraud, and Israel learned centuries later what it costs to break one: the famine in David's day was for Saul's slaughter of these same Gibeonites. Second, God took a people who lied their way into the covenant and set them to serve at His altar for ever. Nethinims stand in Ezra's returning lists. The curse became a place at the house of God.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a drawer as one who draws, particularly one who draws liquor or water; and, in Scripture, a servile labourer.
webster_full: DRAWER, n. One who draws or pulls; one who takes water from a well.
2. He that draws liquor for guests; a waiter in a tavern.
Hewers of wood and drawers of water. Josh. ix.
scriptures: Jos 9:21
And the princes said unto them, Let them live; but let them be hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation; as the princes had promised them.
Jos 9:27
And Joshua made them that day hewers of wood and drawers of water for the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD, even unto this day, in the place which he should choose.
Psa 15:4
In whose eyes a vile person is contemned; but he honoureth them that fear the LORD. He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not.
corruption_summary: An oath is now treated as a statement of present intention, revocable when circumstances change, and the Gibeonite episode is exactly the case Scripture uses to teach the opposite.
corruption_paragraphs: Joshua 9 is the hardest possible test case for the binding force of a vow, and Scripture decides it against Israel's convenience. The league was obtained by lying. Israel was under standing orders to make no covenant with the inhabitants of the land. The princes had failed in the one duty that would have exposed the fraud — they asked not counsel at the mouth of the LORD. Every ground a modern conscience would use to void the agreement was present, and the princes still said, We have sworn unto them by the LORD God of Israel: now therefore we may not touch them. Psalm 15 makes that very disposition a mark of the man who shall abide in God's tabernacle: he that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not. And 2 Samuel 21 shows the cost of the opposite: three years of famine in David's reign because Saul, centuries later, slew the Gibeonites in his zeal, breaking an oath he had not made. Modern practice treats promises — marital, contractual, congregational — as commitments held for as long as they serve the parties. Ecclesiastes 5:5 gives the older wisdom: better is it that thou shouldest not vow, than that thou shouldest vow and not pay. The Gibeonites, meanwhile, are the standing proof that God can put a deceiver to work at His altar and keep him there.
roots_summary: Hebrew sha'ab (H7579), to draw water; chatab (H2404), to cut or hew wood; nathiyn (H5411), the Nethinims, the given ones who served the temple.
roots_lines: Hebrew sha'ab (H7579) — to draw water from a well; the daily labour of the women at evening and of the Gibeonites for ever; Genesis 24:11, Joshua 9:21.
Hebrew chatab (H2404) — to hew or gather wood; the paired half of the proverbial phrase; Joshua 9:21, Deuteronomy 29:11.
Hebrew nathiyn (H5411) — the Nethinims, the given ones, temple servants listed among the returning exiles; Ezra 2:43, Nehemiah 7:46.
usage: “Hewers of wood and drawers of water unto all the congregation” — the sentence on the Gibeonite deceit.
“For the congregation, and for the altar of the LORD” — the servitude assigned to the house of God.
“He that sweareth to his own hurt, and changeth not” — the psalm that vindicates Israel's refusal to break the oath.

pos: n. pl. (those who shear the flock; by extension, the shearing feast that accompanied the work)
etymology: A plain English compound. In the ancient East the shearing was the harvest of a flock-keeping household, and it came with a feast of some scale.
biblical_def: Sheepshearing in Scripture is a season of plenty and, twice, the setting for a great sin. “Judah was comforted, and went up unto his sheepshearers to Timnath” (Gen 38:12) — and on that road he turned aside to a woman he took for a harlot, who was Tamar his daughter in law, and the sons of that shearing feast were Pharez and Zarah. Pharez stands in the genealogy of Christ in Matthew 1. Two years after his sister's violation, “Absalom had sheepshearers in Baalhazor…and Absalom invited all the king's sons” (2Sa 13:23), and he pressed his father to come (2Sa 13:24). David declined and sent the princes; and at the feast, when Amnon's heart was merry with wine, Absalom's servants killed him. Nabal's shearing in 1 Samuel 25 is the third: a churl feasting like a king while refusing bread to the men who had guarded his shepherds, until Abigail rode out with loaves and figs and turned David from bloodshed. Three shearings, three feasts, and in every one the abundance of the season becomes the occasion of the sin. Prosperity is a testing season, and Scripture stations these stories at exactly the point where a household has just been paid.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a sheep-shearer as one that shears or cuts off the wool from sheep, and sheep-shearing as the act of shearing sheep, and the feast made on that occasion.
webster_full: SHEEP-SHEARER, n. One that shears or cuts off the wool from sheep.
SHEEP-SHEARING, n. The act of shearing sheep.
2. The time of shearing sheep; also, a feast made on that occasion.
scriptures: And it came to pass after two full years, that Absalom had sheepshearers in Baalhazor, which is beside Ephraim: and Absalom invited all the king's sons.
And Absalom came to the king, and said, Behold now, thy servant hath sheepshearers; let the king, I beseech thee, and his servants go with thy servant.
Shall I then take my bread, and my water, and my flesh that I have killed for my shearers, and give it unto men, whom I know not whence they be?
corruption_summary: Prosperity is assumed to be a season of safety, and Scripture stations three of its worst sins at exactly the moment a household has been paid.
corruption_paragraphs: It is worth noticing how often the Bible puts a catastrophe at a feast. Judah at Timnath, Absalom at Baalhazor, Nabal at Carmel — three shearings, three tables loaded with the year's increase, and out of them come incest with a daughter-in-law, the murder of a brother, and a household that came within an hour of the sword. Agur asked to be fed with food convenient for him precisely because of this: lest I be full, and deny thee, and say, Who is the LORD? Moses warned Israel before they ever crossed the Jordan that the danger of the land flowing with milk and honey was not famine but forgetting — when thou hast eaten and art full, then beware lest thou forget the LORD. Modern Christian instinct runs the other way. Adversity is expected to be spiritually dangerous and prosperity is expected to be a blessing simply enjoyed, so that a season of increase is met with no particular watchfulness at all. The shearing narratives are the correction. When the wool is in and the wine is out and the heart is merry, that is the hour Amnon died and Nabal boasted; and Abigail's errand shows the remedy — a wise head, a loaded string of asses, and a quick ride toward the trouble.
roots_summary: Hebrew gazaz (H1494), to shear or cut off; gozez, the shearers; mishteh (H4960), a feast, a drinking — the entertainment of the shearing.
roots_lines: Hebrew gazaz (H1494) — to shear a flock, to cut off hair; used of Judah's and Absalom's shearings and of the sheep before her shearers dumb; Genesis 38:12, Isaiah 53:7.
Hebrew mishteh (H4960) — a feast, literally a drinking; the shearing entertainment, and Nabal's feast like the feast of a king; 1 Samuel 25:36, Esther 1:3.
Hebrew tsemer (H6785) — wool; the increase that the shearing brought in; Judges 6:37, Isaiah 1:18.
usage: “Went up unto his sheepshearers to Timnath” — Judah on the road where he met Tamar.
“Absalom had sheepshearers in Baalhazor” — the feast at which Amnon was killed.
“My flesh that I have killed for my shearers” — Nabal's answer to David's young men.

pos: n. pl. (sailors; seamen; men whose trade is the working of a ship)
etymology: Old English scipmann, a ship-man. The Authorized Version distinguishes shipmen (the crew) from the master and owner of the ship.
biblical_def: Solomon had no seafaring tradition, so he borrowed one: “Hiram sent in the navy his servants, shipmen that had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon” (1Ki 9:27), and the fleet at Eziongeber brought gold from Ophir. The other appearance is the shipwreck voyage of Acts 27, and it is a study in itself. The shipmen “deemed that they drew near to some country” at midnight (Act 27:27) and sounded twice; then, under colour of casting anchors out of the foreship, “the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship” in the boat (Act 27:30). Paul, a prisoner and no sailor, saw the manoeuvre for what it was and told the centurion, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved — and the soldiers cut the ropes and let the boat fall off. This is the same chapter in which God had already promised Paul by an angel that there should be no loss of any man's life. The promise was absolute; the means were not optional. God ordains the end and the means together, and Acts 27 is the plainest narrative illustration of that doctrine in the New Testament: a divine guarantee, and a command to keep the crew aboard, in the same night.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a shipman as a seaman or sailor — a term now little used except in the Scriptures.
webster_full: SHIPMAN, n. A seaman or sailor.
The shipmen deemed that they drew near to some country. Acts xxvii.
SHIPMASTER, n. The captain, master or commander of a ship.
scriptures: And Hiram sent in the navy his servants, shipmen that had knowledge of the sea, with the servants of Solomon.
And as the shipmen were about to flee out of the ship, when they had let down the boat into the sea, under colour as though they would have cast anchors out of the foreship,
Paul said to the centurion and to the soldiers, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved.
corruption_summary: A promise of God is repeatedly treated as a reason to neglect the means He appointed, and Acts 27:31 is the standing refutation.
corruption_paragraphs: In Acts 27 God had spoken plainly. An angel had stood by Paul in the night saying, Fear not, Paul; thou must be brought before Caesar: and, lo, God hath given thee all them that sail with thee. Paul believed it and said so publicly: I believe God, that it shall be even as it was told me. Then, a few verses later, when the sailors tried to slip away in the boat, the same Paul said, Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved. There is no contradiction, and the two verses together are one of the clearest lessons in Scripture on decree and means. God ordained that all would live; He also ordained that the crew would stay aboard, that the ropes would be cut, that men would eat before the wreck, and that those who could swim would swim. A fatalism that reasons from God's sovereignty to the neglect of appointed means is not Reformed doctrine but its counterfeit, and it appears everywhere: in the man who will not see a physician because God is able to heal, in the church that will not evangelise because the elect will be saved, in the believer who will not resist a temptation because he is kept by the power of God. The LBCF holds both hands: God ordains whatsoever comes to pass, and yet so as thereby no violence is offered to the will of the creatures, nor is the liberty or contingency of second causes taken away, but rather established.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'anshey 'oniyyot, men of ships; Greek nautes (G3492), a sailor; Greek kubernetes (G2942), the ship's master or steersman.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'oniyyah (H591) — a ship; Hiram's navy and the ship of Tarshish that Jonah found; 1 Kings 9:27, Jonah 1:3.
Greek nautes (G3492) — a sailor, a shipman; the crew of the Alexandrian corn ship in the Adria; Acts 27:27, 27:30, Revelation 18:17.
Greek kubernetes (G2942) — a steersman, the ship's master; whose counsel the centurion preferred to Paul's; Acts 27:11, Revelation 18:17.
usage: “Shipmen that had knowledge of the sea” — Hiram's crews lent to Solomon's navy.
“The shipmen were about to flee out of the ship” — the manoeuvre a prisoner detected.
“Except these abide in the ship, ye cannot be saved” — the promise, and the means.

pos: n. pl. (officers set over a treasury, whether of a king or of the house of God)
etymology: Old French tresorier, from Latin thesaurus, a hoard. The office is one of trust, and Scripture names its qualification in a single phrase: they were counted faithful.
biblical_def: Artaxerxes issued a decree “to all the treasurers which are beyond the river, that whatsoever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, shall require of you, it be done speedily” (Ezr 7:21). A pagan emperor put the imperial treasury at the service of the house of God, and Ezra blessed the LORD who had put such a thing in the king's heart. Nehemiah then set up the office within Israel and named the qualification: “I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah…for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren” (Neh 13:13). Not the ablest, not the wealthiest, not the best connected — counted faithful. Daniel gives the third picture: Nebuchadnezzar gathered “the princes, the governors, and the captains, the judges, the treasurers, the counsellors, the sheriffs, and all the rulers of the provinces” to the dedication of the golden image (Dan 3:2-3). The treasurers stood in that plain of Dura with everyone else, and every officer of the empire bowed except three men. Money is never neutral in Scripture: it is either administered by men counted faithful, or it is standing in rank before an image.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a treasurer as one who has the care of a treasure or treasury; an officer who receives the public money arising from taxes and duties and disburses it by order.
webster_full: TREASURER, n. One who has the care of a treasure or treasury; an officer who receives the public money.
2. In corporations, the officer who receives and disburses the funds of the company.
TREASURY, n. A place or building in which stores of wealth are reposited.
scriptures: Ezr 7:21

And I, even I Artaxerxes the king, do make a decree to all the treasurers which are beyond the river, that whatsoever Ezra the priest, the scribe of the law of the God of heaven, shall require of you, it be done speedily,

And I made treasurers over the treasuries, Shelemiah the priest, and Zadok the scribe, and of the Levites, Pedaiah: and next to them was Hanan the son of Zaccur, the son of Mattaniah: for they were counted faithful, and their office was to distribute unto their brethren.
Moreover it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful.
corruption_summary: Churches and ministries repeatedly appoint over their money the men who are impressive rather than the men who are faithful, and Nehemiah names the only qualification that matters.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 13:13 gives four names and one reason: for they were counted faithful. The office was to distribute unto their brethren, and Nehemiah had just returned to Jerusalem to find that the storerooms had been given to Tobiah the Ammonite and the Levites' portions had not been paid, so that the singers had gone back to their fields and the house of God was forsaken. He knew exactly what unfaithful administration costs. Paul says the same thing of a wider office: it is required in stewards, that a man be found faithful (1Co 4:2), and when the apostles appointed men over the daily ministration in Acts 6 they specified men of honest report, full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom — a spiritual standard for a job that involved bread and widows. The corruption is a persistent habit of appointing on other grounds: the successful businessman by default, the largest donor, the man whose competence is obvious and whose character has never been examined. Ministry finance scandals almost never begin with an incompetent treasurer; they begin with a competent one who was never counted faithful. And the qualification runs both ways, as Nehemiah shows — the same chapter records a leader willing to contend, and curse, and pluck off hair, over money that had been diverted from the house of God.
roots_summary: Aramaic gizbar (H1489), a treasurer; Hebrew 'otsar (H214), a treasury or store; Greek oikonomos (G3623), a steward, a house-manager.
roots_lines: Aramaic gizbar (H1489) — a treasurer; the Persian imperial officers of Ezra 7 and the Babylonian officials of Daniel 3; Ezra 7:21, Daniel 3:2.
Hebrew 'otsar (H214) — a treasury, a store, a magazine; the chambers of the house of God that Nehemiah cleansed; Nehemiah 13:12-13, Malachi 3:10.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward, one set over a household's goods; the New Testament office of trust, and its one requirement; 1 Corinthians 4:2, Titus 1:7.
usage: “A decree to all the treasurers which are beyond the river” — a pagan treasury put at the service of God's house.
“For they were counted faithful” — the whole qualification for the office.
“The judges, the treasurers, the counsellors” — the officers of empire assembled before an image.

pos: n. (a chief secretary or officer of state; in Ezra, the Persian official Rehum who wrote against Jerusalem)
etymology: Late Latin cancellarius, an officer who stood at the cancelli, the lattice screen of a court. The Authorized Version uses the English office-name for the Aramaic be'el te'em, master of decree.
biblical_def: The word belongs to one man and one campaign. “Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king” (Ezr 4:8), joined by a long list of transplanted peoples (Ezr 4:9). The letter is a masterpiece of its kind: it never mentions religion. It warns the king that if this rebellious and bad city be builded again, and the walls set up, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings; and it advises a search of the book of the records to prove Jerusalem's history of sedition. The appeal is entirely to imperial security and money. It worked: the king answered Rehum and Shimshai (Ezr 4:17) and commanded the work to cease, and it ceased unto the second year of Darius. Then God raised up Haggai and Zechariah, and the work began again, and the same search of the records that had stopped it — the roll found at Achmetha with Cyrus' decree — is what set it going. Opposition to the work of God rarely announces itself as opposition to God. It comes as a memorandum about revenue, signed by an official with a legitimate office.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a chancellor as a high judicial or administrative officer of a court or state; originally a chief notary or scribe under emperors and kings.
webster_full: CHANCELLOR, n. Originally a chief notary or scribe, under the emperors; but in England, in later times, an officer invested with judicial powers.
2. The chief judge of a court of equity.
Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem. Ezra iv.
scriptures: Ezr 4:8
Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem to Artaxerxes the king in this sort:
Ezr 4:13
Be it known now unto the king, that, if this city be builded, and the walls set up again, then will they not pay toll, tribute, and custom, and so thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings.
Ezr 5:5
But the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease, till the matter came to Darius: and then they returned answer by letter to the king of Babylon.
corruption_summary: Hostility to the work of God is usually filed as an administrative concern — revenue, security, public order, compliance — and is answered wrongly when treated as a debate about religion.
corruption_paragraphs: Read Rehum's letter carefully and notice what is missing. There is no theology in it. It does not dispute the God of Israel, does not mock the temple, does not raise a single religious objection. It is a competent civil-service memorandum arguing that a rebuilt Jerusalem is a fiscal and security risk to the crown: they will not pay toll, tribute, and custom; search the records; this city is hurtful unto kings and provinces. That is how opposition to the work of God has usually arrived, and how it arrives still — not as an argument about Christ, but as a zoning decision, a licensing requirement, a charity-registration condition, a tax question, an employment rule. Christians frequently answer such things as though a doctrinal debate had been opened, and lose, because the objection was never doctrinal. Ezra shows the pattern of response. The Jews did not win by out-arguing Rehum; the work stopped for years. God raised prophets, the elders resumed building, and when they were challenged again the answer was a search of the archive that produced Cyrus' original decree. Ezra 5:5 is the sentence to hold: the eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews, that they could not cause them to cease.
roots_summary: Aramaic be'el te'em, master of decree or command, rendered chancellor; caphar (H5613), a scribe; Aramaic 'ishparna', speedily, diligently — the word of the later decree that reversed him.
roots_lines: Aramaic be'el te'em — lord of judgment or master of decree; the office title rendered “chancellor”; Ezra 4:8-9, 4:17.
Aramaic caphar (H5613) — a scribe, a secretary; Shimshai who drafted the letter, and the honourable use of the same office in Ezra the scribe; Ezra 4:8, 7:6.
Aramaic 'osparna (H629) — speedily, with diligence; the word in Darius' counter-decree commanding the work to go forward; Ezra 6:8, 7:21.
usage: “Rehum the chancellor and Shimshai the scribe wrote a letter against Jerusalem” — the opposition with a legitimate office.
“Thou shalt endamage the revenue of the kings” — the argument that never mentions God.
“The eye of their God was upon the elders of the Jews” — the answer that outlasted the memorandum.

pos: n. (a written roll or record; in Ezra and Nehemiah, the genealogical roll of the returning exiles)
etymology: Late Latin registrum, from regerere, to record or enter. In Scripture it is always a document of descent, and it decides who may serve.
biblical_def: Nehemiah, moved of God to number the people, says: “I found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first, and found written therein” (Neh 7:5) — and the list follows, family by family, with the number of each. The document mattered because of a specific problem recorded twice in identical words: certain priestly families “sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” (Ezr 2:62; Neh 7:64). Men who believed themselves priests, who had come all the way from Babylon to serve, were barred because the roll did not have them. The Tirshatha ruled that they should not eat of the most holy things till there stood up a priest with Urim and with Thummim. Under the old covenant, descent was everything for the priesthood; a man could not volunteer into Aaron's line. That is precisely the problem the epistle to the Hebrews raises about Christ, who sprang out of Judah, of which tribe Moses spake nothing concerning priesthood — and answers with a priest after the order of Melchisedec, made not after the law of a carnal commandment, but after the power of an endless life. The register was real, and it pointed past itself.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a register as a written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings; a book of public records; also the officer who keeps the record.
webster_full: REGISTER, n. A written account or entry of acts, judgments or proceedings, for preserving and conveying to future times an exact knowledge of transactions.
2. The book of records; a book in which entries are made.
3. The officer or person whose business is to write and keep the register.
scriptures: Neh 7:5

And my God put into mine heart to gather together the nobles, and the rulers, and the people, that they might be reckoned by genealogy. And I found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first, and found written therein,
Ezr 2:62
These sought their register among those that were reckoned by genealogy, but they were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood.
And whosoever was not found written in the book of life was cast into the lake of fire.
corruption_summary: Religious identity is now built on self-description — a man is what he sincerely considers himself to be — and the register stands in Scripture as the refusal of that principle at its most painful.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezra 2:62 is a hard verse and it is meant to be. Men had made the journey from Babylon believing themselves to be priests. They may well have been sincere; nothing in the text calls them liars. But when the roll was searched their names were not in it, and they were put from the priesthood as polluted. Sincerity was not the standard; enrolment was. That principle offends a culture in which identity is understood to be constituted by inward conviction and public declaration, so that to question a man's account of himself is treated as an offence against him. Scripture does not work that way about anything that matters. The Lord Jesus said that many would say to Him in that day, Lord, Lord, have we not prophesied in thy name? — men entirely persuaded of their standing — and His answer is, I never knew you. The book of life in Revelation 20:15 is the register of which Ezra's roll was the shadow, and the same rule governs: not found written. This is not a counsel of despair, because unlike a Babylonian genealogy the book of life is not entered by descent at all, and the way in is published openly — whosoever will, let him take the water of life freely. But it is entered God's way, and a man's certainty about himself is not the register.
roots_summary: Hebrew kethab (H3791), a writing, a register; yachas (H3187), to reckon by genealogy, to enrol; Greek biblos tes zoes, the book of life.
roots_lines: Hebrew kethab (H3791) — a writing, an edict, a register; the roll Nehemiah found; Nehemiah 7:5, Esther 3:14.
Hebrew yachas (H3187) — to reckon by genealogy, to enrol; the verb that decided a priest's standing; Ezra 2:62, 1 Chronicles 5:17.
Greek biblos (G976) — a book, a scroll; the book of life in which names are written from the foundation of the world; Revelation 20:15, Philippians 4:3.
usage: “I found a register of the genealogy of them which came up at the first” — Nehemiah's roll of the returning exiles.
“They were not found: therefore were they, as polluted, put from the priesthood” — sincerity was not the standard.
“Whosoever was not found written in the book of life” — the register of which Ezra's roll was the shadow.

pos: n. (a royal officer charged with keeping the annals and acting as the king's remembrancer)
etymology: From record, Latin recordari, to call to mind, from cor, the heart. The Hebrew mazkir is literally “the one who causes to remember”.
biblical_def: The recorder appears in every list of the great officers of the crown, and always near the top. In David's cabinet: “Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder” (2Sa 8:16), and he is still in place at the end of the reign (2Sa 20:24). In Solomon's: “Elihoreph and Ahiah, the sons of Shisha, scribes; Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud, the recorder” (1Ki 4:3) — the same man serving two kings. In Hezekiah's: when Rabshakeh shouted at the wall, the three men who went out to him were Eliakim who was over the household, Shebna the scribe, and “Joah the son of Asaph the recorder” (2Ki 18:18), and they came back with their clothes rent and told Hezekiah the words. In Josiah's reformation, Joah the recorder is among the three sent to repair the house (2Ch 34:8). The Hebrew title, mazkir, is the remembrancer: his business was that the king should not forget — the annals kept, the deeds recorded, the petitions brought to mind. It was a sleepless remembrancer of this kind that saved the Jews in Esther, when the king could not sleep and commanded the book of records to be read.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a recorder as one whose official duty is to register writings or transactions; one who records or registers; an officer who keeps the rolls.
webster_full: RECORDER, n. A person whose official duty is to register writings or transactions; one who enrolls or records.
2. An officer of a city who keeps the rolls, and whose duty is to certify the proceedings.
3. In Scripture, an officer of the Hebrew kings, a remembrancer or keeper of the annals.
scriptures: And Joab the son of Zeruiah was over the host; and Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder;
And when they had called to the king, there came out to them Eliakim the son of Hilkiah, which was over the household, and Shebna the scribe, and Joah the son of Asaph the recorder.
Est 6:1
On that night could not the king sleep, and he commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles; and they were read before the king.
corruption_summary: A people that keeps no record of what God has done is a people that will not be able to answer its own children, and Scripture makes remembrance a duty rather than a sentiment.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Nobody is arguing about what a recorder was. The principle to recover is the office itself, translated. Israel's kings kept a remembrancer as a matter of state, and Israel as a nation was commanded to do the same thing at the household level: the twelve stones out of Jordan were set up at Gilgal precisely so that when your children shall ask their fathers in time to come, saying, What mean these stones? then ye shall let your children know. The Passover was an annual recorder. The psalms rehearse the exodus for generations that never saw it. Deuteronomy's recurring danger is not apostasy by argument but apostasy by forgetting: beware lest thou forget the LORD. Very few Christian households keep any record at all of what God has actually done among them — the prayers answered, the provisions made, the deliverances, the dates. The result is that a family's memory of God's dealings rarely survives two generations, and each generation begins from nothing. Esther 6:1 is the encouragement: a record faithfully kept, forgotten for years, read out on a sleepless night, and a nation delivered by it.
roots_summary: Hebrew mazkir (H2142 hiphil participle), one who causes to remember, a remembrancer; zakar (H2142), to remember; cepher hazzikronot, the book of records.
roots_lines: Hebrew mazkir — the remembrancer; the participle of zakar, used as the title of the royal recorder; 2 Samuel 8:16, 1 Kings 4:3, 2 Kings 18:18.
Hebrew zakar (H2142) — to remember, to mention, to record; the covenant verb, of God remembering His covenant and of Israel commanded to remember; Genesis 8:1, Deuteronomy 8:2.
Hebrew zikkaron (H2146) — a memorial, a record; the stones, the feasts, and the book of records read to Ahasuerus; Exodus 12:14, Esther 6:1.
usage: “Jehoshaphat the son of Ahilud was recorder” — the same officer under David and Solomon.
“Joah the son of Asaph the recorder” — one of the three who faced Rabshakeh at the wall.
“He commanded to bring the book of records of the chronicles” — a record kept, and a nation delivered.

pos: n. pl. (teachers of the law; the learned rabbis of the temple and the schools)
etymology: Latin doctor, a teacher, from docere, to teach. In the Authorized Version it never means a physician; it always means a teacher.
biblical_def: A boy of twelve was left behind in Jerusalem, and after three days His parents “found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions” (Luk 2:46). The posture is exact and worth noticing: He sat among them, He heard them, and He asked. He did not lecture them. And all that heard him were astonished at his understanding and answers. Luke uses the fuller title later: “there were Pharisees and doctors of the law sitting by, which were come out of every town of Galilee, and Judaea, and Jerusalem: and the power of the Lord was present to heal them” (Luk 5:17) — the scene where the paralytic came through the roof and was forgiven before he was healed. Paul was trained in this class, brought up at the feet of Gamaliel, and Gamaliel himself is called a doctor of the law had in reputation among all the people (Act 5:34). Scripture does not despise learning. It shows an incarnate Lord submitting to the ordinary means of instruction as a boy, and it shows the same learned class, twenty years later, sitting by while the power of the Lord was present to heal and finding fault.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a doctor as a teacher; one who has passed the degrees of a faculty and is empowered to teach; and, in Scripture, an expounder of the law.
webster_full: DOCTOR, n. A teacher; one who has passed all the degrees of a faculty, and is empowered to practice and teach.
2. One skilled in a profession; a man of learning.
They found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors. Luke ii.
scriptures: Luk 2:46
And it came to pass, that after three days they found him in the temple, sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions.
Luk 5:17

And it came to pass on a certain day, as he was teaching, that there were Pharisees and doctors of the law sitting by, which were come out of every town of Galilee, and Judaea, and Jerusalem: and the power of the Lord was present to heal them.
Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm.
corruption_summary: Two errors trade places in every generation: the anti-intellectualism that treats study as the enemy of faith, and the credentialism that treats a degree as a substitute for it.
corruption_paragraphs: Luke 2:46 has been enlisted on both sides of a false quarrel. One party makes the boy in the temple a rebuke to learning — the untaught child confounding the scholars — and builds from it a piety suspicious of study, of languages, of history, of anything that requires work. The text does not support it. He was sitting in the midst of the doctors, hearing them and asking them questions, which is a description of a student in a school, and the astonishment was at His understanding and His answers, not at His contempt for the class. The other party makes the doctors the model and turns the ministry into a guild, in which the question about a teacher is where he studied rather than what he preaches and how he lives. Paul, the best trained man in the New Testament, wrote against that: some desire to be teachers of the law, understanding neither what they say, nor whereof they affirm (1Ti 1:7), and he counted his own considerable credentials loss for Christ. The Reformed tradition has generally held the balance well, insisting on a learned ministry and an open Bible in the plough-boy's hand at the same time. Learning is a servant. Luke 5:17 shows what it looks like when the servant sets up as master: the doctors of the law sitting by, with the power of the Lord present to heal, taking notes on a blasphemy charge.
roots_summary: Greek didaskalos (G1320), a teacher; nomodidaskalos (G3547), a teacher of the law, the fuller title of Luke 5:17; grammateus (G1122), a scribe.
roots_lines: Greek didaskalos (G1320) — a teacher, a master; used of the temple doctors, of the Lord Himself, and of the office in the church; Luke 2:46, John 13:13, Ephesians 4:11.
Greek nomodidaskalos (G3547) — a teacher of the law; used of the doctors sitting by, of Gamaliel, and of those who desire the title without the understanding; Luke 5:17, Acts 5:34, 1 Timothy 1:7.
Greek grammateus (G1122) — a scribe, a man of letters; the professional class of copyists and expounders, repeatedly joined with the Pharisees; Matthew 23:2, Mark 12:28.
usage: “Sitting in the midst of the doctors, both hearing them, and asking them questions” — a boy of twelve in the posture of a student.
“Pharisees and doctors of the law sitting by” — learning present at a miracle and taking offence.
“Desiring to be teachers of the law; understanding neither what they say” — the title without the substance.

pos: n. pl. (traders; men whose business is buying and selling, especially in caravan or by ship)
etymology: From merchant, Old French marchant, from Latin mercari, to trade. The Authorized Version's merchantmen are the men, not the vessels.
biblical_def: The word appears at the darkest moment of Joseph's story: “Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt” (Gen 37:28). A trading caravan on an ordinary commercial route, buying a boy at a discount from his own brothers, carried the future governor of Egypt to the exact place God intended, and Joseph would say to those brothers years later, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. Solomon's revenue included what “he had of the merchantmen, and of the traffick of the spice merchants” (1Ki 10:15). And the Lord Jesus put the trade into a parable that turns it inside out: the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls: who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it (Mat 13:45-46). A merchant is a man who knows values, and the whole point of the parable is a valuation: he did not lose by the sale. He was the only man in the market who had priced the pearl correctly.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a merchantman as a ship employed in commerce; and merchant as one who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who buys and sells goods.
webster_full: MERCHANTMAN, n. A ship employed in the transportation of goods, as distinguished from a ship of war.
MERCHANT, n. A man who traffics or carries on trade with foreign countries, or who exports and imports goods and sells them by wholesale.
The kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man seeking goodly pearls. Matt. xiii.
scriptures: Then there passed by Midianites merchantmen; and they drew and lifted up Joseph out of the pit, and sold Joseph to the Ishmeelites for twenty pieces of silver: and they brought Joseph into Egypt.
Again, the kingdom of heaven is like unto a merchant man, seeking goodly pearls:
Who, when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it.
corruption_summary: The pearl of great price is preached as the cost of discipleship and almost never as what it plainly is — a valuation, in which the man who sold everything got the better end of the trade.
corruption_paragraphs: The parable of the pearl is short enough that every word counts, and the word that governs it is merchant. A merchant is a professional appraiser; his whole living depends on knowing what a thing is worth. When this man sold all that he had, he was not making a sacrifice in the sentimental sense, and he was not being reckless. He was making the trade of his life, and every other dealer in that market who kept his money made the worse bargain. Sermons on this parable regularly turn it into an exhortation about the cost of following Christ, all emphasis on sold all that he had, with the tone of a man being asked to give something up. The Lord's emphasis is on the pearl. Paul preaches the parable in Philippians 3 without mentioning it: what things were gain to me, those I counted loss for Christ — and he goes further, I count all things but loss for the excellency of the knowledge of Christ Jesus my Lord, and do count them but dung, that I may win Christ. That is not a man mourning a sacrifice; that is an appraiser explaining a valuation. Jim Elliot's much-quoted line says the same in a sentence: he is no fool who gives what he cannot keep to gain what he cannot lose. Meanwhile Genesis 37:28 stands as the reminder that God routinely uses the ordinary traffic of trade — a caravan on a schedule, a price agreed at a pit — to move His purposes to the place He has appointed.
roots_summary: Hebrew cachar (H5503), to travel about as a trader; rokel (H7402), a spice merchant, a pedlar; Greek emporos (G1713), a merchant who travels for trade.
roots_lines: Hebrew cachar (H5503) — to go about, to trade; the caravan traders of Genesis 37 and the merchandise of the virtuous woman; Genesis 37:28, Proverbs 31:14.
Hebrew rokel (H7402) — a spice merchant, a trafficker; the traffick that came to Solomon's table; 1 Kings 10:15, Ezekiel 27:22.
Greek emporos (G1713) — a merchant, one who travels for trade; the man seeking goodly pearls, and the merchants of the earth who weep over Babylon; Matthew 13:45, Revelation 18:11.
usage: “There passed by Midianites merchantmen” — an ordinary caravan carrying God's purpose into Egypt.
“Of the merchantmen, and of the traffick of the spice merchants” — the revenue of Solomon.
“A merchant man, seeking goodly pearls” — the appraiser who priced the kingdom correctly.

pos: n. (the master of a house; the head of a family or estate; the standing figure of God in the kingdom parables)
etymology: English household and -er. The Greek oikodespotes is literally the house-despot — the man with undisputed authority over his own estate.
biblical_def: The householder is one of the Lord's recurring figures for God Himself, and every parable that uses him turns on his right to do as he will with his own. The servants of the householder come asking about the tares: “Sir, didst not thou sow good seed in thy field? from whence then hath it tares?” (Mat 13:27) — and he forbids the uprooting until harvest. Every scribe instructed unto the kingdom “is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old” (Mat 13:52) — the faithful teacher holds the Old Testament and the New together and produces both. The householder of Matthew 20:1 “went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard”, and pays the eleventh-hour man a penny, and answers the murmurers, Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good? And the householder of Matthew 21:33 plants a vineyard, hedges it, digs a winepress, builds a tower, lets it out to husbandmen, and goes into a far country — and at last sends his son. Four parables, one figure: an owner with absolute right, whose dealings are always just and frequently more generous than his servants think proper.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a householder as the master or head of a family; one who keeps house with his family; an occupier of a house.
webster_full: HOUSEHOLDER, n. The master or head of a family; one who keeps house with his family.
2. An occupier of a house.
The kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder. Matt. xx.
scriptures: Then said he unto them, Therefore every scribe which is instructed unto the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old.
Mat 20:1
For the kingdom of heaven is like unto a man that is an householder, which went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard.
Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good?
corruption_summary: The parable of the labourers is regularly read as a lesson in fair wages, when its subject is the absolute freedom of God to be generous, and the murmuring it exposes is the murmuring of the long-serving.
corruption_paragraphs: Matthew 20 is read at cross purposes about as often as any parable in the Gospels. Some read it as an economic teaching about equal pay; others read it as evidence that the householder is unfair, and try to soften him. The parable answers both in verse 15, which is the sentence everything else is built to deliver: Is it not lawful for me to do what I will with mine own? Is thine eye evil, because I am good? No one was underpaid — the first-hired agreed with him for a penny and received a penny. The offence was not injustice but generosity to somebody else, and the parable is a precise description of the human heart, which can bear a loss more easily than it can bear another man's undeserved gain. Paul makes the same argument doctrinally in Romans 9 with the potter and the clay, and the objection he anticipates is exactly the murmuring of Matthew 20. This is the confessional doctrine of unconditional election in parable form: God has mercy on whom He will have mercy, and nobody is wronged. It is also a pastoral warning aimed squarely at the long-serving — the elder brother, the labourer who bore the burden and heat of the day, the man who has been in the church forty years and cannot rejoice over a deathbed conversion.
roots_summary: Greek oikodespotes (G3617), the master of a house; oikos (G3624), a house or household; oikonomos (G3623), the steward set under him.
roots_lines: Greek oikodespotes (G3617) — the master of the house, the head of an estate; the standing figure for God in the kingdom parables; Matthew 13:27, 20:1, 21:33.
Greek oikos (G3624) — a house, and by extension a household or family line; the house of God which is the church; 1 Timothy 3:15, Hebrews 3:6.
Greek oikonomos (G3623) — a steward; the servant who administers what the householder owns and answers for it; Luke 16:1, 1 Corinthians 4:2.
usage: “Bringeth forth out of his treasure things new and old” — the instructed scribe holding both Testaments.
“Went out early in the morning to hire labourers into his vineyard” — the parable of the penny.
“Is thine eye evil, because I am good?” — the question that exposes the murmuring of the long-serving.

pos: n. (one who pursues wild game; in Scripture, a character type as much as a trade)
etymology: Old English huntian, to hunt. The Hebrew tsayid covers both the hunting and the venison; a hunter is a man who takes prey.
biblical_def: Scripture names two hunters and neither is a hero. Nimrod “was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD” (Gen 10:9) — and the next verse tells us the beginning of his kingdom was Babel. He is the first empire-builder in the Bible, and the phrase before the LORD is best read as defiant rather than devout, in the face of God. Esau “was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents” (Gen 25:27) — and the very next scene has Esau coming in from the field faint and selling his birthright for a mess of pottage. Hebrews calls him a profane person, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. The third use turns the picture round and puts the reader in the animal's place: “Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler” (Pro 6:5) — the urgency of a man who has become surety for his friend, and by extension of every man caught in a snare he walked into himself. The dictionary draws no rule against hunting from these texts; venison was Isaac's dish. It notes only that Scripture's hunters are men of appetite and dominion, and it watches both.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a hunter as one who pursues wild animals with a view to take them; one who follows the chase.
webster_full: HUNTER, n. One who pursues wild animals with a view to take them, either for sport or for food.
2. A dog that scents game, or is employed in the chase.
3. A horse used in the chase.
scriptures: Gen 10:9
He was a mighty hunter before the LORD: wherefore it is said, Even as Nimrod the mighty hunter before the LORD.
And the boys grew: and Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field; and Jacob was a plain man, dwelling in tents.
Pro 6:5
Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter, and as a bird from the hand of the fowler.
corruption_summary: Esau is regularly made the sympathetic brother and Jacob the villain, which inverts the judgment Scripture itself passes in Malachi, Romans, and Hebrews.
corruption_paragraphs: A popular way of reading Genesis 25 and 27 makes Esau the wronged outdoorsman and Jacob the schemer who stole what was not his, and there is enough in the narrative to make the reading tempting: Jacob's dealing was crooked, Rebekah's scheme was crooked, and Scripture reports both without excusing either. But the Bible passes its own verdict on the brothers, and it is not the sympathetic one. Malachi 1:2-3, quoted by Paul in Romans 9:13, says Jacob have I loved, but Esau have I hated, and Paul's explicit point is that the choice was made before the children were born, neither having done any good or evil, that the purpose of God according to election might stand. Hebrews 12:16 adds the moral characterisation: lest there be any fornicator, or profane person, as Esau, who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright. The word is profane — a man to whom nothing was holy, who could trade a covenant blessing for a bowl of soup because he genuinely could not see the difference in value. That is the sin the text is exposing, and the modern retelling misses it entirely by asking who behaved better at dinner. God's election is not a reward for good behaviour; Jacob's deceit proves it as thoroughly as Esau's appetite does.
roots_summary: Hebrew tsayid (H6718), hunting, game, venison; gibbor tsayid, a mighty one of the hunt; yaqosh (H3369), to lay a snare, whence the fowler of Proverbs 6:5.
roots_lines: Hebrew tsayid (H6718) — the chase, and the venison taken in it; Nimrod the mighty hunter, and Isaac's love of Esau's venison; Genesis 10:9, 25:28.
Hebrew tsuwd (H6679) — to hunt, to lie in wait for; used of hunting men as well as beasts; Genesis 27:5, Micah 7:2.
Hebrew yaqosh (H3369) — to ensnare, to lay bait; the fowler from whose snare the soul escapes; Proverbs 6:5, Psalm 124:7.
usage: “A mighty hunter before the LORD” — and the beginning of his kingdom was Babel.
“Esau was a cunning hunter, a man of the field” — set against Jacob dwelling in tents.
“Deliver thyself as a roe from the hand of the hunter” — the reader put in the animal's place.

pos: n. pl. (those who chase after; in Joshua, the men of Jericho hunting the spies)
etymology: Old French porsuir, from Latin prosequi, to follow after. In Scripture the pursuers are almost always searching for someone God has hidden.
biblical_def: Rahab hid the two spies under the stalks of flax on her roof, sent the king's men off toward the fords, and gave the spies their instructions: “Get you to the mountain, lest the pursuers meet you; and hide yourselves there three days, until the pursuers be returned: and afterward may ye go your way” (Jos 2:16). They obeyed, “and abode there three days, until the pursuers were returned: and the pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not” (Jos 2:22). A harlot in a doomed city outwitted her own king's search parties, and she did it because she had heard what the LORD did to the Red sea and confessed, the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath. She is in Hebrews 11 among the heroes of faith and in Matthew 1 in the genealogy of Christ. The word appears once more, at Ai, where the ambush turned the battle: “the people that fled to the wilderness turned back upon the pursuers” (Jos 8:20). The men of Ai had been drawn out by a feigned flight, and the moment the smoke of their city rose behind them, the fleeing men turned. In both scenes the pursuers are confident, numerous, and entirely mistaken about who is being hunted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a pursuer as one who follows with a view to overtake; one who chases; a plaintiff or prosecutor in some legal usage.
webster_full: PURSUER, n. One who follows with a view to overtake or apprehend; one who chases.
2. In Scotland, a plaintiff; a prosecutor.
PURSUE, v.t. To follow; to go or proceed after or in a certain course; to chase.
scriptures: Jos 2:16
And she said unto them, Get you to the mountain, lest the pursuers meet you; and hide yourselves there three days, until the pursuers be returned: and afterward may ye go your way.
Jos 2:22
And they went, and came unto the mountain, and abode there three days, until the pursuers were returned: and the pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not.
Jos 2:11

And as soon as we had heard these things, our hearts did melt, neither did there remain any more courage in any man, because of you: for the LORD your God, he is God in heaven above, and in earth beneath.
corruption_summary: Rahab is treated either as an embarrassment to be explained away or as proof that Scripture excuses a lie, and both readings miss what Hebrews and James actually commend in her.
corruption_paragraphs: Rahab poses a genuine question that Christian ethics has argued for centuries: she deceived the king's pursuers, and she is commended. The two easy answers are both wrong. The first sanitises her, insisting that she cannot really have lied or that a Canaanite could not be expected to know better; the text is not embarrassed and calls her Rahab the harlot in three separate books. The second concludes that Scripture permits falsehood whenever the cause is good, which is a rule no one could safely hold and which the Bible's own condemnations of lying will not support. The New Testament tells us precisely what was commended, and it is neither her trade nor her tongue. Hebrews 11:31: by faith the harlot Rahab perished not with them that believed not, when she had received the spies with peace. James 2:25: was not Rahab the harlot justified by works, when she had received the messengers, and had sent them out another way? The commended thing is the receiving and the sending — that she threw in her lot with the people of God against her own city, at the risk of her life, on the strength of what she had heard about the Red sea. Her confession in Joshua 2:11 is better theology than most of Israel managed in the wilderness, and the scarlet line in the window is one of the plainest pictures of the passover blood in the Old Testament.
roots_summary: Hebrew radaph (H7291), to pursue, to chase, to persecute; baqash (H1245), to seek, to search out; tiqvah (H8615), a line or cord — the scarlet thread in the window.
roots_lines: Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue, chase, or persecute; the king's men after the spies, and goodness and mercy that shall follow me all the days of my life; Joshua 2:16, Psalm 23:6.
Hebrew baqash (H1245) — to seek, to search diligently; the pursuers sought them throughout all the way; Joshua 2:22, Jeremiah 29:13.
Hebrew tiqvah (H8615) — a cord, and also hope; the scarlet line Rahab bound in the window is the same word as the hope of Israel; Joshua 2:18, Jeremiah 29:11.
usage: “Lest the pursuers meet you” — a harlot directing the LORD's spies past her own king's search.
“The pursuers sought them throughout all the way, but found them not” — confident, numerous, and mistaken.
“The people that fled to the wilderness turned back upon the pursuers” — the ambush at Ai.

pos: n. pl. (those who flee; refugees, deserters, or escapees, according to context)
etymology: Latin fugitivus, from fugere, to flee. The word carries both pity and reproach in Scripture, and the two are seldom far apart.
biblical_def: The word is first an insult. The men of Ephraim, quarrelling with Gilead after Jephthah's victory, taunted them: “Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim among the Ephraimites, and among the Manassites” (Jdg 12:4) — a slur about ancestry and belonging that ended in forty-two thousand Ephraimites dead at the fords of Jordan over the pronunciation of one word. Then it is a category of judgment: at the fall of Jerusalem, “the fugitives that fell away to the king of Babylon” were carried away by Nebuzaradan with the rest (2Ki 25:11) — deserting to the winning side did not save them. Then it is an object of pity: “My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar” (Isa 15:5), and the prophet who pronounces the burden of Moab weeps over it. And finally it is a sentence: “all his fugitives with all his bands shall fall by the sword” (Eze 17:21), on Zedekiah who broke his oath to Babylon. Scripture's attitude toward the man in flight is therefore never simple, and the law had already settled the practical question long before: the cities of refuge stood open, and the escaped servant was not to be delivered up to his master.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a fugitive as one who flees from danger, pursuit, duty or service; a deserter; one who has fled or escaped from his country.
webster_full: FUGITIVE, n. One who flees from his station or duty; a deserter; one who flees from danger.
2. One who has fled or deserted and taken refuge under another power, or one who has fled from punishment.
3. One hard to be caught or detained; that which is fleeting and unstable.
scriptures: Jdg 12:4

Then Jephthah gathered together all the men of Gilead, and fought with Ephraim: and the men of Gilead smote Ephraim, because they said, Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim among the Ephraimites, and among the Manassites.
Isa 15:5

My heart shall cry out for Moab; his fugitives shall flee unto Zoar, an heifer of three years old: for by the mounting up of Luhith with weeping shall they go it up; for in the way of Horonaim they shall raise up a cry of destruction.
Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped from his master unto thee:
corruption_summary: Scripture's treatment of the man in flight is regularly flattened into one policy or another, when the Bible gives a settled duty toward the fleeing and a settled refusal to make his flight a proof of innocence.
corruption_paragraphs: The Bible speaks about fugitives more often than most readers realise, and it never speaks in one register. There is a plain duty of refuge: the escaped servant is not to be handed back but is to dwell where it liketh him best, and thou shalt not oppress him (Deu 23:15-16); six cities stood open across the land for the man who had killed unawares; the stranger within the gates is protected in the law again and again, and Israel is told why — ye were strangers in the land of Egypt. And there is an equally plain refusal to treat flight as a verdict: the cities of refuge held a trial, and the manslayer who proved to be a murderer was delivered up to the avenger of blood. Zedekiah's fugitives fled from an oath he had sworn by God. The modern discussion tends to collapse this into a single posture — either that every fleeing person is by definition innocent and owed everything, or that the fleeing are by definition guilty and owed nothing. Scripture holds both duties without embarrassment: shelter the fugitive, and judge the case. Isaiah 15 shows the temper the church should have while doing it, and it is not neutrality. The prophet announcing Moab's destruction says, My heart shall cry out for Moab.
roots_summary: Hebrew paliyt (H6412), an escaped one, a fugitive; naphal (H5307), to fall away, to desert; miqlat (H4733), a refuge, the cities of refuge.
roots_lines: Hebrew paliyt (H6412) — an escaped one, a fugitive; used of the man who brought Abram word, and of Moab's refugees; Genesis 14:13, Isaiah 15:5.
Hebrew naphal (H5307) — to fall, and idiomatically to fall away or desert to an enemy; the fugitives that fell away to Babylon; 2 Kings 25:11, Jeremiah 39:9.
Hebrew miqlat (H4733) — a refuge, an asylum; the six cities appointed for the man who fled; Numbers 35:11, Joshua 20:2.
usage: “Ye Gileadites are fugitives of Ephraim” — a slur about belonging that cost forty-two thousand lives.
“His fugitives shall flee unto Zoar” — the prophet weeping over the nation he condemns.
“Thou shalt not deliver unto his master the servant which is escaped” — the law of refuge.

pos: n. pl. (those who grieve; also the hired professional mourners of an eastern funeral)
etymology: Old English murnan, to grieve. In the ancient East mourning was a public office as well as a private grief, with professionals who went about the streets.
biblical_def: Job, describing the days of his greatness, says he “dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners” (Job 29:25) — a great man's dignity measured by his presence in other people's sorrow. The Preacher paints old age and death in a series of failing images and ends with the funeral: “man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets” (Ecc 12:5) — the professional mourners, whose trade is grief, on their way to another house. Isaiah then gives the promise: “I have seen his ways, and will heal him: I will lead him also, and restore comforts unto him and to his mourners” (Isa 57:18), and the next verse creates the fruit of the lips, Peace, peace, to him that is far off, and to him that is near. Hosea gives the warning: sacrifices offered by an unrepentant people shall be unto them “as the bread of mourners; all that eat thereof shall be polluted” (Hos 9:4) — food eaten in a house of death was ceremonially unclean, and their worship had become that. Over all of it stands the second beatitude, which promises exactly what Isaiah promised: Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a mourner as one that mourns or is grieved at any misfortune; one that follows a funeral in the habit of mourning; one who is hired to mourn at a funeral.
webster_full: MOURNER, n. One that mourns or is grieved at any misfortune.
2. One who follows a funeral in the habit of mourning.
3. Something used at funerals; and among the ancients, one hired to mourn.
scriptures: I chose out their way, and sat chief, and dwelt as a king in the army, as one that comforteth the mourners.
Ecc 12:5

Also when they shall be afraid of that which is high, and fears shall be in the way, and the almond tree shall flourish, and the grasshopper shall be a burden, and desire shall fail: because man goeth to his long home, and the mourners go about the streets:
I have seen his ways, and will heal him: I will lead him also, and restore comforts unto him and to his mourners.
corruption_summary: Grief is now managed as a psychological process to be moved through efficiently, and the church has largely lost the older practice of sitting with mourners and saying nothing for a long time.
corruption_paragraphs: Scripture gives grief room that our culture does not. Israel mourned Jacob seventy days and Moses thirty; Job's friends sat with him on the ground seven days and seven nights, and none spake a word unto him, for they saw that his grief was very great — which is the best thing they ever did and the last. The modern instinct is to treat mourning as a process with stages and an expected duration, and to consider a griever who is still grieving after some reasonable interval as stuck. Congregations feel this as an unspoken clock: casseroles for two weeks, then the expectation that ordinary conversation may resume. Two things are lost. The first is the ministry Job describes as the crown of his greatness, one that comforteth the mourners — which in Scripture generally means presence rather than explanation. The second is hope, because a culture that hurries grief is usually a culture that cannot say anything true about death. Paul does not tell the Thessalonians not to sorrow; he tells them not to sorrow as others which have no hope, and then he gives them the resurrection in five verses and says, comfort one another with these words. Blessed are they that mourn: for they shall be comforted. The comfort is promised to the mourning, not to those who moved on quickly.
roots_summary: Hebrew 'abel (H57), a mourner, one in mourning; caphad (H5594), to beat the breast, to lament; Greek pentheo (G3996), to mourn, of the second beatitude.
roots_lines: Hebrew 'abel (H57) — mourning, a mourner; Job's ministry to them, and Isaiah's promise to comfort all that mourn; Job 29:25, Isaiah 61:2-3.
Hebrew caphad (H5594) — to beat the breast, to wail; the professional lamentation of an eastern funeral; Ecclesiastes 12:5, Jeremiah 16:6.
Greek pentheo (G3996) — to mourn, to grieve openly; the second beatitude, and Paul's word for the church that should have mourned over sin; Matthew 5:4, 1 Corinthians 5:2.
usage: “As one that comforteth the mourners” — Job's description of his own greatness.
“The mourners go about the streets” — the professionals of grief in the Preacher's funeral.
“Restore comforts unto him and to his mourners” — the promise that stands behind the beatitude.

pos: n. pl. (those invited to a table; in Scripture, the invited of a feast whose host determines everything)
etymology: Old Norse gestr, a guest, cognate with Latin hostis. In the Authorized Version the guests are always defined by the host who bade them.
biblical_def: Adonijah's coronation feast at Enrogel is the first scene: “Adonijah and all the guests that were with him heard it as they had made an end of eating” (1Ki 1:41), and when the news came that Solomon had been anointed at Gihon, “all the guests that were with Adonijah were afraid, and rose up, and went every man his way” (1Ki 1:49). A table full of men committed to a usurper emptied in a moment when the true king was crowned. The second is Wisdom's rival: the foolish woman has her own house, her own table, and her own invitation, Stolen waters are sweet — “But he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell” (Pro 9:18). Two houses, two suppers, two guest lists, and Proverbs 9 sets them side by side on purpose. The third is Zephaniah: “Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord GOD: for the day of the LORD is at hand: for the LORD hath prepared a sacrifice, he hath bid his guests” (Zep 1:7) — and in that terrible passage the guests are invited to a sacrifice in which Judah is the victim. Scripture's last word on the subject is the marriage supper of the Lamb, and the beatitude attached: Blessed are they which are called unto the marriage supper of the Lamb.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a guest as a stranger or friend entertained in the house or at the table of another; a visitor; one who is entertained.
webster_full: GUEST, n. A stranger or friend entertained in the house or at the table of another, whether by invitation or otherwise; a visitor.
2. A stranger or person who lodges at an inn or tavern.
The LORD hath prepared a sacrifice, he hath bid his guests. Zeph. i.
scriptures: And all the guests that were with Adonijah were afraid, and rose up, and went every man his way.
Pro 9:18
But he knoweth not that the dead are there; and that her guests are in the depths of hell.
Zep 1:7
Hold thy peace at the presence of the Lord GOD: for the day of the LORD is at hand: for the LORD hath prepared a sacrifice, he hath bid his guests.
corruption_summary: Both houses in Proverbs 9 send out the same invitation in the same words, and a generation trained to choose by preference has no way to tell them apart.
corruption_paragraphs: Proverbs 9 is built as a deliberate pair, and the symmetry is the whole point. Wisdom has builded her house, hewn out her seven pillars, killed her beasts, mingled her wine, furnished her table, and sent forth her maidens to cry upon the highest places of the city. The foolish woman is clamorous, simple, and knoweth nothing, and she sits at the door of her house on a seat in the high places of the city. Then they both call, and the words are identical: Whoso is simple, let him turn in hither. The invitations are indistinguishable by their form. Only the outcomes differ — forsake the foolish, and live, on the one hand; her guests are in the depths of hell, on the other. That is a devastating passage for an age which chooses its beliefs, its companions and its loves by the appeal of the invitation, and which has been taught that the authentic desire of the heart is the most reliable guide available. Proverbs answers that the desire is exactly what is being competed for, that both callers know it, and that both will offer sweetness. The chapter gives one instrument of discrimination and one only, and it is verse 10: the fear of the LORD is the beginning of wisdom. Adonijah's guests found out the same thing more cheaply than most — they discovered whose table they were at only when the trumpet sounded for the true king.
roots_summary: Hebrew qara' (H7121), to call, to invite; qaruw', the called ones, the bidden guests; Greek kletos (G2822), called, invited — the word behind the marriage supper.
roots_lines: Hebrew qara' (H7121) — to call, to summon, to invite; the LORD bidding His guests to the sacrifice; Zephaniah 1:7, 1 Samuel 9:13.
Hebrew rapha'iym (H7496) — the dead, the shades; who are in the house of the foolish woman without the guests' knowledge; Proverbs 9:18, 2:18.
