Greek kletos (G2822) — called, invited; the many called and the few chosen, and the blessed who are called to the marriage supper; Matthew 22:14, Revelation 19:9.
usage: “All the guests that were with Adonijah were afraid” — a usurper's table emptied by a trumpet.
“Her guests are in the depths of hell” — the other house in Proverbs 9, with the same invitation.
“He hath bid his guests” — a sacrifice in which the nation is the victim.

pos: n. (goods, merchandise offered for sale); also, in Luke 8:27, an archaic past tense of wear
etymology: Old English waru, goods, merchandise. The identical spelling in Luke 8:27 is a different word entirely — the old past tense of wear — and readers regularly confuse them.
biblical_def: The word belongs to Nehemiah's sabbath reform. The covenant the people sealed included this clause: “if the people of the land bring ware or any victuals on the sabbath day to sell, that we would not buy it of them on the sabbath, or on the holy day” (Neh 10:31). Years later Nehemiah came back and found the covenant broken: men of Tyre dwelling in the city “which brought fish, and all manner of ware, and sold on the sabbath unto the children of Judah” (Neh 13:16). He testified against them, shut the gates at dark, set his servants there, and when “the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice” (Neh 13:20) he warned them that if they did it again he would lay hands on them. The traders were foreigners; the covenant-breakers were Judah, who bought. A separate word of identical spelling appears at Gadara, where the man with the legion “ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs” (Luk 8:27) — there ware is simply the old past tense of wear, and the man was later found sitting at the feet of Jesus, clothed, and in his right mind.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines ware as goods; commodities; merchandise; usually in the plural, wares — and separately as the obsolete preterit of wear.
webster_full: WARE, n. Goods; commodities; merchandise; usually in the plural.
But in some cases it is used in the singular; as, all manner of ware.
WARE, the obsolete preterit of wear, now written wore.
scriptures: And if the people of the land bring ware or any victuals on the sabbath day to sell, that we would not buy it of them on the sabbath, or on the holy day: and that we would leave the seventh year, and the exaction of every debt.
So the merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem once or twice.
Luk 8:27
And when he went forth to land, there met him out of the city a certain man, which had devils long time, and ware no clothes, neither abode in any house, but in the tombs.
corruption_summary: The Lord's Day has been quietly surrendered to commerce, and the surrender happened the way Nehemiah's did — not by argument, but by buying.
corruption_paragraphs: Nehemiah 13 is a study in how a covenant dies. Nobody in Jerusalem voted to repeal chapter 10. The men of Tyre simply came in with fish, and Judah simply bought, and after enough sabbaths the practice was the norm and the clause was a dead letter. Nehemiah's response is instructive and entirely unfashionable: he contended with the nobles, asked what evil thing is this that ye do, and pollute the sabbath day? — and then he did something structural. He commanded the gates shut at dark before the sabbath and set his own servants at them, so that no burden could be brought in. Conviction was backed by a lock. The dictionary holds the fourth commandment as a creation ordinance and the Lord's Day as the Christian sabbath, and it holds also that the day is a delight and not a burden — the sabbath was made for man. What has happened in most of the English-speaking church is a repeat of Nehemiah 13 in slow motion: no argument was lost, the day was simply spent. Sunday commerce, Sunday sport, Sunday work chosen rather than required. The remedy in Nehemiah was not a new doctrine; it was a decision about the gates. Households that have recovered the day generally report that they did it the same way, by shutting something at dark.
roots_summary: Hebrew maqqachah (H4728), merchandise, wares for sale; rakal (H7402), to traffick, to trade; Greek enduo (G1746), to put on clothing — behind the unrelated ware of Luke 8:27.
roots_lines: Hebrew maqqachah (H4728) — merchandise, wares offered for sale; used only in Nehemiah's sabbath covenant; Nehemiah 10:31.
Hebrew mekar / rakal (H7402) — merchandise, to traffick; the sellers of all kind of ware lodging outside the gates; Nehemiah 13:16, 13:20.
Greek enduo (G1746) — to clothe, to put on; the Gadarene who wore no clothes, and Paul's command to put on the Lord Jesus Christ; Luke 8:27, Romans 13:14.
usage: “If the people of the land bring ware…we would not buy it of them on the sabbath” — the sealed covenant.
“The merchants and sellers of all kind of ware lodged without Jerusalem” — conviction backed by a shut gate.
“Ware no clothes, neither abode in any house” — the other ware, the old past tense of wear.

pos: n. (a place of public buying and selling; in Ezekiel, the trading floor of Tyre)
etymology: Latin mercatus, trade, a market, from mercari, to trade. Ezekiel's lament over Tyre is the longest sustained commercial passage in Scripture.
biblical_def: Ezekiel 27 is a merchant's inventory turned into a funeral song. Nation after nation brings its goods to Tyre: “Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market” (Eze 27:13) — slaves listed between the metalwork and the horses, in the same tone; “Judah, and the land of Israel, they were thy merchants: they traded in thy market wheat of Minnith, and Pannag, and honey, and oil, and balm” (Eze 27:17); bright iron, cassia and calamus in her market from Dan and Javan (Eze 27:19); “The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas” (Eze 27:25). Then the east wind breaks her in the midst of the seas, and the same merchants who sang hiss at her. The chapter that follows names the sin under the commerce: by the multitude of thy merchandise they have filled the midst of thee with violence, and thou hast sinned; and, thine heart was lifted up because of thy beauty. Tyre was not judged for trading. She was judged for what the trading did to her heart, and for what she was willing to sell.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines a market as a public place in a city or town where provisions or cattle are exposed to sale; also the rate of purchase and sale, and a place of resort for buyers and sellers.
webster_full: MARKET, n. A public time and appointed place of buying and selling; also, purchase and sale.
2. A public building in which provisions are exposed to sale; a market-house.
3. Rate of purchase and sale; price; as, the market is high or low.
scriptures: Javan, Tubal, and Meshech, they were thy merchants: they traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market.
The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market: and thou wast replenished, and made very glorious in the midst of the seas.
And cinnamon, and odours, and ointments, and frankincense, and wine, and oil, and fine flour, and wheat, and beasts, and sheep, and horses, and chariots, and slaves, and souls of men.
corruption_summary: The market is treated as a morally neutral mechanism whose outcomes cannot be judged, when Scripture judges markets precisely by what is on the list.
corruption_paragraphs: Ezekiel 27:13 and Revelation 18:13 are the same accusation four centuries apart, and both work by the placement of a single item in an inventory. Ezekiel lists slaves — the persons of men — between vessels of brass and horses. John, cataloguing the merchandise of Babylon, runs through cinnamon, odours, ointments, frankincense, wine, oil, fine flour, wheat, beasts, sheep, horses, chariots, and then, last and deliberately, slaves, and souls of men. Neither prophet argues. Both simply read out the manifest and let the position of the human beings in it do the work. That is Scripture's method of judging a market, and it is neither the doctrinaire condemnation of commerce nor the modern assumption that a market is a neutral mechanism which cannot be morally assessed because it merely reflects what people want. The Bible everywhere honours honest trade: it commands just weights and balances, praises the virtuous woman who is like the merchants' ships, and shows Lydia a seller of purple hosting the church at Philippi. What it will not grant is that a transaction is justified by being voluntary. The test it applies is what is being sold, at what cost to whom, and what the selling has done to the seller's heart — and by that test Tyre, in all her glory in the midst of the seas, was already condemned while the ships of Tarshish were still singing.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'arab (H4627), merchandise, that which is exchanged; cachar (H5503), to trade, to go about as a merchant; Greek gomos (G1117), a ship's cargo, merchandise.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'arab (H4627) — merchandise, an exchange; the word repeated through the Tyre lament and rendered “market”; Ezekiel 27:13, 27:19, 27:25.
Hebrew cachar (H5503) — to travel about as a trader, to traffick; Tyre's merchants and the merchandise of wisdom, which is better than silver; Ezekiel 27:12, Proverbs 3:14.
Greek gomos (G1117) — a cargo, freight, merchandise; the manifest of Babylon that ends with slaves, and souls of men; Revelation 18:11-13, Acts 21:3.
usage: “They traded the persons of men and vessels of brass in thy market” — the accusation made by an inventory.
“The ships of Tarshish did sing of thee in thy market” — glory in the midst of the seas, already condemned.
“And slaves, and souls of men” — the same charge in the last book of the canon.

pos: n. (the act of waiting on or serving; the state of being present in service; also the body of attendants)
etymology: Latin attendere, to stretch toward, from ad- and tendere. To give attendance is to stretch the whole mind toward a thing, not merely to be in the room.
biblical_def: The queen of Sheba, having seen Solomon's wisdom, the house he had built, the meat of his table, the sitting of his servants, “and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD” — had no more spirit in her (1Ki 10:5; the Chronicler repeats it in 2Ch 9:4). The ordered service of a king's household took her breath away, and a greater than Solomon is here. Paul then applies the word to the ministry: “Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” (1Ti 4:13) — three duties, in that order, and the verb means to apply oneself, to hold oneself to a thing. Reading is the public reading of Scripture; exhortation is the pressing of it on the conscience; doctrine is the teaching of it in order. Hebrews then uses the word negatively of the tribe of Judah, “of which no man gave attendance at the altar” (Heb 7:13) — nobody from Judah ever served as a priest, which is exactly the argument: Christ's priesthood is not from Aaron but from Melchisedec, and the change of priesthood requires a change of law. Attendance in Scripture is never mere presence; it is service given with the whole attention.
webster_summary: Webster (1828) defines attendance as the act of waiting on or serving; a waiting on; also, the persons attending; a train; a retinue.
webster_full: ATTENDANCE, n. The act of waiting on, or serving.
2. A waiting on; a being present on business of any kind; as, attendance on public worship.
3. The persons attending; a train; a retinue.
scriptures: And the meat of his table, and the sitting of his servants, and the attendance of his ministers, and their apparel, and his cupbearers, and his ascent by which he went up unto the house of the LORD; there was no more spirit in her.
Till I come, give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.
Heb 7:13
For he of whom these things are spoken pertaineth to another tribe, of which no man gave attendance at the altar.
corruption_summary: Attendance has shrunk to a headcount — a metric of who was in the room — and the biblical sense of applying the whole mind to a service has largely gone with it.
corruption_paragraphs: The English word has narrowed badly. In 1611 to give attendance meant to apply oneself, to hold to a duty with the whole mind; today attendance is a number on a sheet. That shrinkage has consequences in the church, where attendance figures became for a generation the primary measure of health, and where the question asked of a member is whether he was present rather than what he attended to. Paul's charge to a young pastor is the corrective, and its order repays attention: give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine. Reading first — the public reading of the Scriptures aloud in the assembly, a practice largely displaced in modern services by everything else; then exhortation, pressing the word on the conscience; then doctrine, teaching it in order. All three are the word, handled three ways, and the same chapter tells Timothy to meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them; that thy profiting may appear to all. That is what attendance means. The queen of Sheba was not counting Solomon's servants when her spirit failed her; she was watching how they served.
roots_summary: Hebrew ma'amad (H4612), a station, an attendance, the standing-place of servants; Greek prosecho (G4337), to hold toward, to give heed, to apply oneself; Greek prosecho tini, to attend to a duty.
roots_lines: Hebrew ma'amad (H4612) — a station, a post of attendance; the ordered standing of Solomon's ministers that overcame the queen of Sheba; 1 Kings 10:5, 2 Chronicles 9:4.
Greek prosecho (G4337) — to hold one's mind toward, to give heed, to devote oneself; Paul's charge to Timothy, and the same verb for giving heed to seducing spirits; 1 Timothy 4:13, 4:1.
Greek prosecho in Hebrews 7:13 — to give attendance at the altar, of priestly service; the argument that Christ's priesthood is not Aaronic; Hebrews 7:13-14.
usage: “The attendance of his ministers, and their apparel” — the ordered service that took the queen's breath.
“Give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine” — the pastor's charge, in that order.
“Of which no man gave attendance at the altar” — Judah, and a priesthood after another order.
